conversation.content:
**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in postpartum mental health.**  
I’m grateful you’ve taken the time to meet with me today. We’re going to complete the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**—a brief, ten‑question screening tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week since your baby arrived.  

Your responses are completely confidential, and this is a safe, non‑judgmental space where you can share whatever is on your mind. The EPDS is simply a way for us to get a clearer picture of your emotional wellbeing so we can offer the right support, whether that’s reassurance, resources, or a referral for further care.

We’ll go through the ten questions one at a time, and you can answer as honestly as feels comfortable. There are no right or wrong answers—just your experience.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.

**First question:**  
*In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?*
In the past week I’ve found it hard to laugh or see the funny side of things—​I’d say it’s **not quite so often**.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Actually, I’m still finding it hard to laugh or see the funny side of things. Most days I feel low‑energy and a bit sad, and even when something is meant to be light‑hearted I just don’t feel that lift. It’s not that I’m trying to hide it—I just don’t get the same enjoyment I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’ve been looking forward to things only **hardly ever** these past few days. It feels like most activities just pass without the excitement or pleasure I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
I’ve blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong **some of the time** over the past week. It’s not every single moment, but I do notice those thoughts popping up more often than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I’ve been anxious or worried for no good reason **quite often** over the past week. The thoughts keep looping—especially about my baby’s safety—and even when I try to calm myself, the worry doesn’t always go away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’ve felt scared or panicky for no very good reason **quite often** during the past week. It’s usually a sudden rush of fear that comes out of nowhere, especially when I’m trying to get my baby settled or when I’m alone at night.
Things have been getting on top of me
Things have been getting on top of me **some of the time** over the past week. I do feel overwhelmed at moments, but I’m still managing to take care of the baby and get through the day.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
I’ve been so unhappy that I’ve had difficulty sleeping **quite often** this past week—I’ve struggled to fall asleep on several nights and wake up a couple of times with anxious thoughts.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve felt sad or miserable **quite often** during the past week. It’s a low mood that hangs around most days, even when I’m trying to focus on the baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I’ve been crying **some of the time**—usually once or twice a week when I feel especially stressed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
I’ve had thoughts of harming myself, but only **hardly ever**—maybe once or twice in the past week, and I haven’t felt any real plan or intention to act on them.

I hear how overwhelming this time has been for you. You've shared that you rarely feel able to laugh or see the funny side of things, that looking forward to activities feels hard, that you sometimes blame yourself when things go wrong, that worry about your baby's safety and sudden panic episodes happen quite often, that you're struggling with sleep, feeling sad and miserable, crying a few times a week, and that you've had a few passive thoughts of harming yourself. <quote>I've been so unhappy that I've had difficulty sleeping</quote> and <quote>I've felt sad or miserable quite often</quote> are especially painful, and it's understandable to feel exhausted and distressed. You are not alone and help is available.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports being unable to laugh or see the funny side, matching the 'Not at all' option</sym>, <sym>Patient reports looking forward to things only hardly ever, matching 'Hardly at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming themselves 'some of the time', matching the 'Yes, some of the time' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling anxious/worried quite often, matching 'Yes, very often' option</sym>, <sym>The response indicates feeling overwhelmed 'some of the time', matching the option 'Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad or miserable quite often, matching the 'Yes, quite often' option.</sym>, <sym>the option 'Only occasionally'. This option is reverse‑scored, giving a score of 2.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 18 exceeds the threshold of 14, indicating probable postpartum depression and triggering an urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. Multiple items reflect core depressive symptoms: loss of pleasure (Q1, Q2), persistent sadness (Q8), crying (Q9), and impaired sleep (Q7). Anxiety and panic symptoms are prominent (Q4, Q5) and align with the anxiety component often seen in postpartum mood disorders. The presence of passive self‑harm thoughts (Q10) adds a safety concern. According to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, the patient exhibits at least five depressive symptoms-including depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, and psychomotor changes-lasting more than two weeks and occurring during the postpartum period, supporting a provisional impression of postpartum depression with anxiety features. This screening highlights the need for immediate clinical follow‑up and safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with a <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med> or a <med>postpartum mental health specialist</med>
2. Complete a full clinical assessment for <med>postpartum depression</med> and anxiety, including a diagnostic interview
3. Develop a safety plan addressing the passive self‑harm thoughts and identify supportive contacts
4. Implement sleep hygiene strategies and consider brief counseling or therapy for anxiety and panic symptoms
5. Provide information about local <med>postpartum support groups</med>, crisis helpline numbers, and parenting resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: **Screening Summary – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety Check**

**Client ID:** [Redacted] **Date:** 2025‑10‑07 **Clinician:** [Name, LCSW]

---

### 1. Reported Symptoms & Emotional/Behavioral Concerns
| Domain | Client’s Report | Frequency/Intensity |
|--------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Anhedonia / Low pleasure** | Difficulty laughing or seeing the funny side; loss of enjoyment in activities | “Hardly ever” to “some of the time” (past week) |
| **Anticipatory pleasure** | Rarely looks forward to events or activities | “Hardly ever” (past few days) |
| **Self‑blame / Guilt** | Unnecessary self‑blame when things go wrong | “Some of the time” (past week) |
| **Anxiety / Worry** | Persistent worry, especially about baby’s safety; looping thoughts | “Quite often” (past week) |
| **Panic / Sudden fear** | Sudden, unexplained fear episodes, often when caring for baby or alone at night | “Quite often” (past week) |
| **Overwhelm** | Feelings of being “on top of” tasks, but still managing daily care | “Some of the time” (past week) |
| **Sleep disturbance** | Difficulty falling asleep, multiple awakenings with anxious thoughts | “Quite often” (past week) |
| **Sadness / Low mood** | Persistent sad or miserable mood | “Quite often” (past week) |
| **Crying spells** | Crying 1–2 times per week, usually linked to stress | “Some of the time” |
| **Suicidal ideation** | Passive thoughts of self‑harm, no plan or intent | “Hardly ever” (1–2 episodes in past week) |

---

### 2. Consistent Patterns Across Answers
- **Low mood and loss of pleasure** are reported across multiple items (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9).  
- **Anxiety‑related symptoms** (worry, panic, feeling overwhelmed) appear frequently (Q4‑Q6).  
- **Sleep disruption** is linked to mood and anxiety (Q7).  
- **Self‑blame** is present, though not pervasive.  
- **Passive self‑harm thoughts** are present, albeit infrequent and without intent.

---

### 3. Areas of Screening Significance (Postpartum Depression & Anxiety)
- **Anhedonia / Diminished interest** – core symptom of postpartum depression.  
- **Persistent sadness / crying** – indicates depressive affect.  
- **Sleep disturbance** – common in both postpartum depression and anxiety.  
- **Excessive worry & panic** – suggest postpartum anxiety or panic disorder features.  
- **Feelings of being overwhelmed** – may reflect impaired coping or adjustment stress.  
- **Self‑blame / guilt** – contributes to depressive cognitions.  
- **Passive suicidal ideation** – safety risk, requires immediate attention.

---

### 4. Risk Factors & Safety Flag
- **Mood‑related risk:** Frequent sadness, loss of pleasure, crying spells.  
- **Sleep‑related risk:** Insomnia with anxious awakenings.  
- **Anxiety/panic risk:** Recurrent, intrusive worry about infant safety; sudden panic episodes.  
- **Self‑harm risk:** Passive thoughts of self‑injury reported “hardly ever” (1–2 instances) – **flagged as a safety concern**; requires further safety assessment and monitoring.

---

### 5. Clinical Observation (Screening Note)
- The client reports a **consistent low mood**, **marked reduction in enjoyment**, and **frequent crying**, all occurring **more than half of the past week**.  
- **Anxiety symptoms** (excessive worry, panic‑type fear) are present **quite often**, with specific focus on infant safety and nighttime alone periods.  
- **Sleep is disrupted** by both mood and anxiety, with difficulty initiating sleep and early‑night awakenings.  
- **Self‑blame** is noted intermittently, suggesting maladaptive cognitions but not pervasive guilt.  
- **Passive suicidal ideation** has emerged **hardly ever** (1–2 episodes) without plan or intent; this warrants **immediate safety follow‑up** and documentation per standard protocol.  

**Overall impression:** The client exhibits multiple symptom clusters consistent with **postpartum depressive and anxiety symptomatology**, with **sleep disturbance** and **passive self‑harm thoughts** representing notable risk factors. No formal diagnosis is rendered at this screening level; further comprehensive assessment is recommended, including a formal depression/anxiety scale, safety planning, and possible referral for postpartum mental‑health services.
